catalog_quote: Minor syllables did not occur freely outside of feet formed with a following major syllable; however, a few highly common function words are structurally identical with minor syllables with /ə/ and can be considered as such. ... One notes that 之 *tə did not bear stress in the Odes (Kennedy 1939). This behavior is normal if one thinks of the above forms as minor syllables. Nevertheless we treat them here as a particular type of full syllables. ... There were no tones in Old Chinese (see the discussion in section 5.1). Major syllables were stressed, and any minor syllables were unstressed. This gave disyllabic words an iambic, weak-strong, rhythm. In verse, disyllables and monosyllables alike counted for one foot: a four-foot verse could consist of any combination of monosyllabic and disyllabic words. ... Meanwhile, Pulleyblank (1973, 1977–1978) abandoned his previous vowel-length solutio…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every fragment of the deciding quotation, the domain quote and the exception quote is verbatim in the held B&S 2014 text layer at pp.52-53 (sec. 3.3.1), and the the secondary-stress rule's Pulleyblank passage at p.69; locators match. (2) The classification rests on the current standard reconstruction monograph (2014), held with publisher text; Glottolog's grammars are syntax-only works on Classical Chinese and its top phonology (Baxter 1992) is the superseded predecessor; no better stress source exists or can exist for a reconstructed language. (3) The one open item found and downloaded (Zhuang, Zhao & Feng 2025, works from a monosyllabic bimoraic-foot premise and is silent on stress within sesquisyllabic roots while agreeing that function words are unstressed; Kennedy 1939, Schuessler 2015/B&S 2017, Sagart 1999 and Salmons & Zhua

sources.citation: Zhuang, Huibin, Pusong Zhao & Shengli Feng. 2025. Foot-shift and disyllabification in the history of Chinese: with a revisit of syllabic structures of Old Chinese. Language and Linguistics 26(1): 123-154. doi:10.1075/lali.00173.zhu (open access, CC BY 4.0).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Works in Feng Shengli's prosodic framework: Old Chinese is treated as a 'bimoraic foot language' in which a (heavy) monosyllable constitutes a foot and carries stress ('if monosyllables can carry stresses independently, then this means that monosyllables must have a bimoraic structure', p.131); 'most function words in Old Chinese have yin-type rhymes, which either occupy the unstressed positions or are prosodically invisible constituents' (p.131). Fn.3 (p.128): 'Baxter & Sagart (2014) assume Old Chinese to have been a disyllabic or sesquisyllabic language ... their constructions do not gainsay
sources.note: Open-access prosodic account of OC foot structure (monosyllabic bimoraic foot; function words unstressed); shows the sesquisyllabic premise is not consensus but does not contradict the classification.
